newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore leaders raise pressure on activist Tang.
newsitem.headline: Singapore leaders raise pressure on activist Tang.

text.p: Singapore's political leadership has increased the pressure on opposition politician Tang Liang Hong with more suits for defamation.
Legal notices in the Straits Times newspaper on Friday announced fresh suits against Workers' Party activist Tang by the city-state's Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew.

One notice charged that Tang slandered Lee in the hearing of Ahmad Osman, a Straits Times journalist, on January 23, and then libelled the former prime minister in an article written by Ahmad in the newspaper on January 24.
Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong took action against Tang on Thursday over the same article.
A second notice made similar claims against Tang over remarks to Straits Times reporter Brendan Pereira on January 10 and an article in the newspaper on January 11.

Lee's claims bring to nine the number of suits for defamation against Tang by Singapore's political leadership since the country's general election on January 2, in which the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) won 81 of 83 parliamentary seats.
Tang was an unsuccessful candidate in a hotly contested constituency in the poll and left Singapore after the election saying he had received death threats.
He is currently in London and was unavailable for comment on Friday but has said he intends to fight the lawsuits and eventually return to Singapore.
Tang is being sued separately for defamation by Lee, Goh and nine other members of the PAP, for comments he had made during the election campaign.
The Straits Times story on January 24 quoted Tang commenting on the earlier defamation suits and alleging the legal action against him was politically motivated.
In the article on January 11, Tang was quoted as saying he feared being arrested if he returned to Singapore.
He said he did not discount being arrested under the country's Internal Security Act, which allows police to arrest and detain a person without trial for up to two years at a time.
Lee's latest writs claim unspecified costs against Tang and gave him eight days to respond to the defamation claims.
As in some previous suits, Tang's wife, Teo Siew Har, was cited as a co-defendant in the writs. She was not mentioned in either Straits Times articles and has shunned media attention.
Spouses are sometimes cited as co-defendants in such suits if a court suspects some of a principal defendant's assets may be in their partner's name, a Singapore lawyer told Reuters.

Teo was prevented from leaving Singapore for Malaysia on Monday. The Home Affairs Ministry later said the tax authorities thought she may have been involved in the administration of Tang's tax matters, which were being investigated.

The PAP leaders obtained a court injunction on Monday to block disposal of assets belonging to Tang and Teo worldwide unless they set aside up to S$11.2 million (US$7.94 million) for possible damages and legal costs.
The PAP leaders filed the original defamation suits against Tang for calling them "liars" during the election campaign.

During the campaign Goh had called Tang a "Chinese chauvinist" dangerous to Singapore's racial harmony. Tang denied the charges and filed police reports saying the allegations were groundless and intended to harm his reputation.
